newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sees sanctions chilling investment in Iran.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees sanctions chilling investment in Iran.

text.p: U.S. State Department officials said Wednesday the threat of sanctions against foreign companies had chilled investment in Iran's oil and gas industry over the last year.

"It is notable that during the first year of ILSA (Iran Libya Sanctions Act) there has not been any activity that we have been able to learn about or identify that would be sanctionable under ILSA," said Alan Larsen, Assistant Secretary of State for economic and business affairs.

Larsen spoke at a House International Relations Committee hearing to review the first year of the law that called for the United States to slap sanctions on any foreign company that invested $40 million or more a year in the oil and gas sectors of Iran and Libya.
Pointing to Iran's effort to attract investment in 11 oil and gas projects over the last year, Larsen said no deals had been signed yet.
"So we do think it has had a chilling effect on foreign investment in Iran's petroleum sector," he said.
Congress passed the law last year seeking to increase pressure on Iran and Libya to stop their alleged support of terrorism, acquisition of nuclear weapons, and violations of human rights.

State Department officials said while the U.S. policy had successfully deterred big new investments in Iran, they said Washington would have a better chance of changing Iran's behavior if it had more cooperation from European allies.
"We would have better success were we not acting unilaterally," said David Welch, assistant secretary for Near East Affairs.

Larsen said the State Department was "very closely" watching a proposed transaction by a German bank to finance development of an oil field in Iran. He said the United States did not have enough details yet to decide whether the bank, WestLB, should be penalized under the law.
"We've been sufficiently concerned about the reports that we've raised it with the bank as well as with the German government," Larsen said.
The German Economics Ministry said last weekend it would support WestLB's decision to grant the loan to Iran's Offshore Engineering and Construction Company.
The U.S. government is also following French oil giant Total SA's negotiations to developed the South Pars natural gas field in Iran.

"We have made clear to Total as well as to the French government at very high levels that we will take appropriate action under ILSA if we find that sanctionable activity has occured," Larsen said. "The information that we have at this stage suggests that this deal has not been finalized."

The U.S. officials said they were confident that Turkey would not run afoul of the sanctions law in its mammoth gas supply deal with Iran and Turkmenistan. Last August, Turkey signed a $23 billion, 23-year gas import deal with Iran. But Larsen said it appeared that Turkey was now going to buy that gas from Turkmenistan and would only use Iran as a pipeline route for the gas.
"Our assurance from the Turkish government is that they are going to be buying gas from Turkmenistan, not from Iran," Larsen said.
